A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RePIC study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete Appendices A–D support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original personalized-captioning experiments, grounding scores, GPT-4o preference evaluations, component ablations, and training analyses in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds caption-quality metrics, component ablations, misleading-text evaluations, diversity measurements, Gemini judging, and a synthetic-training-data comparison.

M1.justification: The Qwen2.5-VL/GRPO framework, OCT, VLT, single/multi-ICT rewards, detailed prompts, and length regularization are retained. Expanded descriptions of parameter freezing and ICT length gating document the existing framework rather than establish a changed algorithm. The revised GRPO equation is assessed under T1.

E1.justification: The principal datasets and concept-count settings remain. Appendix C.3 adds scenarios with deliberately misleading textual demonstrations, distinct from v1's mismatched reference-image tests. Appendix C.10 adds DreamBench++ as an alternative synthetic training source.

E2.justification: v2 Table 6 adds the zero-shot Qwen control to the ablation comparison corresponding to v1 Table 4, reusing scores already reported in Table 2. The principal external baseline set remains unchanged; Gemini is an additional evaluator, not a competing captioning method.

E3.justification: v2 substantially broadens evaluation beyond grounding scores and GPT-4o preferences. Section 4.1.3 introduces generated reference captions and seven caption-quality metrics. Appendix C adds misleading-text overlap measurements, diversity evaluation with an anti-copying prompt, and Gemini preference judging, establishing several distinct additional evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: v2 extends leave-one-component-out ablations with ICT-only, OCT-only, and VLT-only variants in Table 6. New analyses test copying under misleading text, output diversity, sensitivity to the model judge, and synthetic training-data quality in Tables A.8–A.10, Figure A.16, and Table A.12.

E5.justification: Section 4.1.3 newly reports generating GPT-4o reference captions with three different seeds. This concerns reference generation, not additional RePIC training runs. The existing training-reward mean and standard-deviation reporting across random seeds in Figure 5 is retained.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises RePIC retrieval F1 from 92.1/79.2/96.1 to 90.4/76.3/94.4 for MyVLM/YoLLaVA/DreamBooth; Table 2 revises two-concept retrieval F1 from 95.6 to 95.7. Substantial new results cover caption quality, copying, diversity, component isolation, Gemini preferences, and synthetic-data sensitivity. The new quality results show mixed rankings, including best METEOR and CLIPScore but lower CIDEr and ImageReward than zero-shot.

T1.justification: Equation 1 is revised to explicitly include token averaging within each response. Appendices C.1–C.2 add the PPO objective and an explicit normalized-advantage formula. This is a limited formal expansion; the GRPO/PPO discussion supplies explanations rather than new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: an RL-based personalization framework using verifiable rewards, reduced dependence on annotated captions, and stronger multi-concept generalization than SFT baselines. Additional evaluations support these existing claims without redefining their main scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds qualifications about model-judge bias, distinguishes textual overlap from caption quality, and acknowledges untested retrieval cases where stored concepts are absent from the query. It also explains ICT reward hacking and attributes synthetic-data sensitivity to image fidelity. The central RL-versus-SFT interpretation remains.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C newly specify the frozen vision encoder and reference policy, ICT-only length gating, multilingual Faker names, crop filtering without augmentation, and more retrieval details. Appendix D separates single- and multi-concept evaluation prompts. Existing hardware, LoRA settings, training budget, and code links remain; these are documentation refinements rather than demonstrated implementation changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for captioning and diversity metrics, DreamBench++, SDXL, and FLAN. Appendix B.4 also adds a novelty assertion about identifying a stable data/instruction composition. The principal related-work discussion and positioning against SFT personalization methods remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section structure are retained. v2 adds Section 4.1.3 and several appendix subsections, expands technical explanations, improves some cross-references, reorganizes prompt material, and updates author/contact and conference text. This is targeted expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with two caption-quality tables, three copying/diversity tables, a synthetic-data comparison table, and the Gemini preference figure. It also expands the ablation and evaluation-template tables. Existing qualitative figures and plots are largely retained and relocated or renumbered.

improvement.justification: The added caption-quality metrics, second model judge, robustness analyses, and implementation explanations strengthen validation beyond v1's grounding and GPT-4o preference evidence. The gain is limited by reporting inconsistencies: Appendix C.3 overstates superiority over RAP-Qwen on Table A.9, and Tables A.11–A.12 retain retrieval scores inconsistent with revised Table 2. Overall, the evidence becomes more informative, but its presentation still needs reconciliation.
